source_text:
Καὶ τάχα τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ἅμα τῇ ἀπαλλαγῇ σχῆμα ὁμοειδὲς ὂν τῷ παχεῖ καὶ
γηΐνῳ σώματι δύναται οὕτως λαμβάνεσθαι. Εἴ ποτε γοῦν ἱστόρηταί τις τῶν
κεκοιμημένων φαινόμενος, ὅμοιος ἑώραται τῷ ὅτε τὴν σάρκα εἶχε σχήματι. Εἶτα·
Ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ Σαμουὴλ φαινόμενος, ὡς δῆλόν ἐστιν, ὁρατὸς ὢν, παρίστησιν ὅτι σῶμα
περιέκειτο· μάλιστα ἐὰν ἀναγκασθῶμεν ὑπὸ τῶν ἀποδείξεων τὴν οὐσίαν τῆς ψυχῆς
ἀσώματον εἶναι καὶ ταύτην ἀποφήνασθαι.
orientation: Origen is explaining how a departed soul can appear visibly, using Samuel as an example.
pass_a_gloss: And perhaps the form of the soul at the same time as the departure, being similar in appearance to the coarse and earthly body, can be taken in this way. If ever at any rate it has been recorded that one of those who have died appeared, he was seen similar to the form which he had when he had the flesh. Then: But also Samuel, appearing, as is clear, being visible, presents that he was clothed with a body; especially if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal and to declare this.

choices.term: ὁμοειδὲς ὂν τῷ παχεῖ καὶ γηΐνῳ σώματι
choices.english: being of the same kind as the coarse and earthly body
choices.why: Keeps the philosophical force of ὁμοειδές as 'same-kind' rather than 'similar', and renders παχεῖ as 'coarse' to preserve the contrast with the soul's incorporeal substance.
rejected: similar to the thick and earthly body
of one form with the gross and earthy body

choices.english: of those who have fallen asleep
choices.why: Preserves the standard early Christian euphemism for the dead, which matters because Origen is discussing the state of the departed.
The middle voice of περίκειμαι means 'to have around oneself'; 'clothed with' captures the sense that the body is a garment the soul wears, which fits Origen's argument.

choices.english: we are compelled by the proofs
choices.why: Keeps the passive force of ἀναγκασθῶμεν with ὑπό + genitive as the agent, showing the proofs exert compulsion on the interpreter.
rejected: we are forced by the demonstrations

choices.term: τὴν οὐσίαν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀσώματον εἶναι
choices.english: the substance of the soul to be incorporeal
choices.why: Uses the fixed glossary term 'incorporeal' for ἀσώματος and 'substance' for οὐσία, which is the standard philosophical rendering.
rejected: the essence of the soul to be bodiless
the being of the soul to be without body

bible_refs.note: Samuel appearing to Saul after his death; Origen cites this as evidence that a departed soul can be seen with a bodily form.

pass_b_english: Perhaps the form the soul takes at its departure can be understood in this way: it resembles the coarse and earthly body. Whenever one of those who have died is reported to have appeared, he has been seen resembling the form he had while he still possessed flesh.

Then again, Samuel also, when he appeared, was visible, as is clear, and this shows that he was clothed with a body. This is especially so if the proofs compel us to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal, and to declare this.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening sentence by separating the soul's form from the comparison to the earthly body, made the logic of Samuel's visible appearance explicit, and smoothed the final clause so the conditional relationship is easier to follow.

notes.why: What proofs compel declaring soul incorporeal? Unstated philosophical arguments
notes.fix: Add note: 'proofs' = Platonic arguments for soul's immateriality

notes.quote: the substance of the soul to be incorporeal
notes.why: Contradicts argument: author wants soul to have bodily form, yet 'compelled' to say incorporeal
notes.fix: Check Greek: may mean 'non-carnal' not 'without any body'

notes.quote: being of the same kind as the coarse and earthly body
notes.why: Awkward phrasing; 'same kind' may mislead about the soul-body relationship.
notes.fix: Render as 'resembling the form of the coarse and earthly body.'

notes.quote: especially if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal
notes.why: Logic seems inverted: Samuel's visible appearance would argue against incorporeality, not for it.
notes.fix: Check the Greek; likely 'even if' or 'although' rather than 'especially if.'

polish.changed: Clarified that the author is speaking throughout, made the logical connection between Samuel's visible appearance and the soul's bodily form explicit, and preserved the conditional clause about the soul's incorporeal substance as the author's own argumentative concession rather than a contradiction.

notes.quote: This is especially so if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal.
notes.why: Unclear if author speaks, quotes opponent, or is ironic; seems to contradict own argument
notes.fix: Clarify: author quoting Origenist position he rejects

notes.quote: declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal
notes.why: Contradicts argument that soul has bodily form; likely author quoting opponent's view
1 Samuel 28 (witch of Endor) alluded to without citation; reader may not recognize

notes.quote: it is of the same kind as the coarse and earthly body
notes.why: Ambiguous: soul's form is 'same kind' as coarse body? Contradicts 'incorporeal' later
notes.fix: Clarify: 'resembling, though finer than, the coarse body'

notes.why: Reference to 1 Samuel 28 (witch of Endor) is not identified; reader cannot place it.
notes.fix: Add reference: 'Samuel, summoned by the witch of Endor (1 Sam. 28).'

notes.quote: the substance of the soul to be incorporeal
notes.why: Philosophical claim about soul's nature appears without context; unclear why 'compelled by proofs.'
notes.fix: Note this refers to philosophical arguments that the soul is non-bodily.

notes.quote: if we are compelled by the proofs to declare
notes.why: Unclear who 'we' are and what 'proofs' compel this declaration; author or a cited source?
notes.fix: Identify whether this is Methodius' own voice or a reported argument.

notes.quote: the substance of the soul to be incorporeal
notes.why: If soul is incorporeal, appearing 'clothed with a body' seems contradictory; argument unclear.
notes.fix: Clarify the logical relationship between incorporeality and visible appearance.

polish.changed: Clarified that Samuel's appearance refers to the Old Testament account in 1 Kingdoms 28 LXX, and rendered 'bodily shape' as 'body' to avoid implying a contradiction with the soul's incorporeal substance.

notes.why: No citation given; reader won't know this is 1 Samuel 28 (witch of Endor).
Context argues soul is 'incorporeal' yet 'clothed with body'—contradictory unless 'body' means 'bodily form'; may mislead.
notes.fix: Clarify: 'invested with a bodily shape' not physical body.

notes.quote: compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal
notes.why: 'Proofs' is vague; likely refers to philosophical arguments about the soul's nature.

problems.quote: it is of the same kind as the coarse and earthly body
problems.why: Contradicts next sentence: soul's form resembles body but is 'incorporeal' substance.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'similar in appearance to' not 'same kind as'.

problems.quote: This is especially so if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal
problems.why: Sentence contradicts itself: Samuel 'clothed with body' vs. 'substance...incorporeal'.
problems.fix: Clarify argument structure: visible form despite incorporeal essence.

problems.quote: this is especially so if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal.
problems.why: The logical connection is unclear: how does Samuel's visible body especially support incorporeality?
problems.fix: Rephrase to clarify the argument's direction.

edits.old: it is of the same kind as the coarse and earthly body
edits.new: it resembles the coarse and earthly body

edits.old: This is especially so if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal.
edits.new: This is especially so if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal and yet to affirm this.

fixed: The first problem is real: 'same kind as' overstates the Greek ὁμοειδὲς, which means 'of like form/appearance', not identity of substance. Changed to 'resembles'.

The second problem is real: the English omitted the force of ταύτην ἀποφήνασθαι, which refers back to declaring the soul's substance incorporeal. Added 'and yet to affirm this' to clarify the argument.
The third problem is addressed by the same edit: the added clause makes clear that Samuel's visible body is especially significant if one must affirm the soul's incorporeal substance.

problems.why: Context argues soul is 'incorporeal' yet 'clothed with body'—contradictory unless 'body' means 'bodily form'; may mislead.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'invested with a bodily shape' not physical body.

problems.quote: compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal
problems.why: 'Proofs' is vague; likely refers to philosophical arguments about the soul's nature.

edits.old: he was clothed with a body
edits.new: he was invested with a bodily shape

fixed: The first problem is real: 'clothed with a body' suggests a physical body, which conflicts with the soul's incorporeality; 'invested with a bodily shape' better conveys the Greek σῶμα περιέκειτο as a body-like form.
The second problem is real: 'proofs' is too vague; 'demonstrations' better renders ἀποδείξεων as philosophical arguments.

problems.why: 'Invested' is archaic and ambiguous; means 'clothed with' but may suggest financial or ecclesiastical meaning.
Vague plural noun with no antecedent; probably means 'arguments' or 'proofs' but sounds like public protests.

problems.quote: This is especially so if we are compelled by the demonstrations to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal and yet to affirm this.
problems.why: Sentence contradicts itself: compelled to declare soul incorporeal yet affirm it has a body; logical connection missing.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'This seems contradictory if we hold the soul incorporeal, yet we must affirm it.'

edits.old: he was invested with a body
edits.new: he was clothed with a body

edits.old: This is especially so if we are compelled by the demonstrations to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal and yet to affirm this.
edits.new: This is especially so if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal and yet to affirm that it was clothed with a body.

fixed: Changed 'invested with a body' to 'clothed with a body' to avoid archaic ambiguity.
Changed 'the demonstrations' to 'the proofs' to match the source term ἀποδείξεων and avoid the public-protest connotation.
Clarified the final sentence by making explicit that the affirmation concerns the soul being clothed with a body, resolving the apparent contradiction.

problems.why: 'Fallen asleep' and 'departure' are both euphemisms for death; reader may miss equivalence
problems.fix: Gloss 'fallen asleep' as 'died' or note equivalence

variants.text: the soul takes at its departure

problems.quote: This is especially so if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal and yet to affirm this
problems.why: Unclear who 'we' is; author? Methodius? Origen? Reader loses argumentative thread
problems.fix: Identify speaker: 'Methodius argues that we are compelled...'

problems.quote: This is especially so if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal and yet to affirm this
problems.why: Sentence contradicts itself: 'incorporeal' yet 'clothed with a body' unresolved
problems.fix: Clarify the paradox: soul is incorporeal in substance yet appears embodied

edits.old: Whenever one of those who have fallen asleep is reported to have appeared, he has been seen resembling the form he had while he still possessed flesh.
edits.new: Whenever one of those who have died is reported to have appeared, he has been seen resembling the form he had while he still possessed flesh.

edits.old: This is especially so if we are compelled by the proofs to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal and yet to affirm this.
edits.new: This is especially so if the proofs compel us to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal and yet to affirm that it appeared with a body.

fixed: The glossary problem about 'fallen asleep' is real: the English used a euphemism that obscured the equivalence with 'departure,' so I changed it to 'died.'

The speaker problem is not a separate issue from the unreadable problem: the sentence is Origen's own reasoning, and the 'we' is the author's inclusive 'we.' The real issue was the unresolved paradox, which I clarified by making explicit that the soul appeared with a body despite being incorporeal in substance.

problems.quote: and yet to affirm that it appeared with a body
problems.why: The source ends by declaring the soul's substance incorporeal ('and to declare this'). English invents a clause about the soul appearing with a body, changing the sense.
problems.fix: This is especially so if the proofs compel us to declare the substance of the soul incorporeal, and to state this openly.

edits.old: This is especially so if the proofs compel us to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal and yet to affirm that it appeared with a body.
edits.new: This is especially so if the proofs compel us to declare the substance of the soul to be incorporeal, and to declare this.

fixed: The Greek ends with 'καὶ ταύτην ἀποφῆναι' (and to declare this), referring back to declaring the soul's substance incorporeal. The English added 'and yet to affirm that it appeared with a body', which is not in the source. Fixed by replacing the final clause with 'and to declare this.'

last_rejected.why: Glossary requires 'departure' for ἀπαλλαγή; 'fallen asleep' obscures the technical term.
last_rejected.ruling: κεκοιμημένων means 'fallen asleep' (deceased); glossary issue about ἀπαλλαγή is irrelevant to this correct rendering.

last_rejected.quote: resembling the form he had while he still possessed flesh
last_rejected.source_quote: ὅμοιος ἑώραται τῷ ὅτε τὴν σάρκα εἶχε σχήματι
last_rejected.why: Source says 'seen similar to the form when he had flesh,' not 'resembling the form he had while he still possessed flesh'—the English adds 'still' which implies temporal continuation not in source.
last_rejected.fix: seen similar to the form he had when he had flesh
last_rejected.ruling: τὴν σάρκα εἶχε = 'had flesh'; 'still possessed' is natural English for past possession, no meaning change.
